body: The kickoff comes in off the radio on the workbench from a long way west: a thin crowd in the Oakland Coliseum, a Cleveland man calling it over the hum of the Stroh’s fridge, and down on the concrete the space heater ticking up to orange at Jack’s shins. The colored lights are still strung along the pegboard, one blue bulb still dead in the middle. The Stroh’s fridge is still shut. There is one new thing out here since Christmas. Over the bench, between the pegboard and the Sunoco calendar, the 1964 program hangs in a gallon freezer bag, the Browns and the Colts in their old colors behind the plastic, and the thumbtacks go through the bag at the corners and not through the program.
“You hung it up,” Jack said, coming in.
“Theo said keep it out of the light.”
“It’s in a freezer bag.”
“It’s out of the light,” Frank said, and that was the end of that.

Frank has the bucket, turned over, and the thermos. Jack has the chair with the duct tape on the seat. His father is still in his church shirt, the sport coat hung on a nail by the side door over the snow shovel, and the Browns hat is back on his head where it lives. On Cleveland’s first punt, while the man on the radio follows the ball downfield, Frank says one thing.
“He looks good.”
He says it to the radio. The radio goes to a commercial for a tire place in Elyria.

He spent the Saints game at the kitchen table, mostly, with the RAZR face up beside the plate of leftover struffoli, a thousand miles from the Dome and Lena in her father’s seats, and Ma at the stove asking every time it buzzed who that was. “The Saints.” “The Saints are texting you.” “They’re losing, Ma.” At that she turned around from the sauce and crossed herself for them, on general principle, and turned back. At four he brought the phone out here. Now, with the Browns on and the heater going, he thumbs back to the top of the afternoon and comes down through it, hers and his.

response: In Oakland the Browns hold them on third down, and at the commercial Frank pours the thermos lid full and looks down into it.
“The Saints girl lose?”
“Overtime.”
Frank drinks. “That’s worse.” He looks into the lid. “She send the coffee? Christmas?”
“Yeah.”
“Good coffee,” Frank says, and the game comes back.

After that it’s the Browns. Harrison up the middle for four, up the middle for six, up the middle for nothing, a West Coast crowd so thin the radio can pick out one man in it yelling about the officials. At the half Frank goes in through the side door and comes back with two plates of Ma’s leftovers under foil and hands Jack one without saying anything, and they eat off their knees with the plates steaming. Neither of them brings up the morning. In the third quarter it starts to snow a little past the window over the bench, small and dry, and Frank watches it a while and says the Oakland weather is wasted on Oakland.

At a quarter past seven the radio gives it to them: Browns 23, Raiders 9. By then the windows over the bench have gone black and the space heater has the garage nearly warm, and the colored lights are most of the light there is. Frank stands up off the bucket, reaches across the bench, and pulls the radio’s plug out of the wall.
“Three straight.”
That’s the call.

response.text: Three straight. I watched the last two minutes through the window of a sports bar in Encino. A man in a Browns hat inside and I made eye contact through the glass. We will never speak of it.

body: The tree is the only light. The house went up at half past ten, Ma last, trying the side door twice, and left the front room to the tree and the furnace and Nonna, who wouldn’t go. She’s asleep in her chair by the window with her head against the wing of it and Theo’s cashmere up under her chin, four feet from where Jack sits on the rug with his back against the couch and *The Moviegoer* open on his knee. She breathes slow and a little loud, in, and then a long time out. The tree puts its colors on the ceiling. Every so often the furnace starts up somewhere under the floor, and the ornaments on the low branches turn a little in the warm air and settle.
At ten past eleven the RAZR goes against his leg. LENA. He has it open before the second buzz, his hand cupped around the bottom of it.
“Hey,” he says, low.

“Hey yourself.” Her voice comes out of the phone full size, a Sunday’s worth of it, and behind it the house on Dupre Street: a television, a cabinet door, Remy saying a linebacker’s name like a curse word. “Why are we whispering?”
“My grandmother’s asleep four feet away.”
On her end a screen door opens on its spring and slaps shut, and the house drops to a murmur behind it. A board creaks, a step taking her weight.
“Then I’ll whisper too,” she whispers.

And she does. He has heard her shout down a seminar, and sing in a basement, and win an argument about a pope at one in the morning. He has never heard her whisper. It turns out to be a different voice altogether, all breath and edges, the New Orleans worn down to the vowels, and it comes from a back step on Dupre Street right up against his ear. He sits very still on his grandmother’s rug and keeps the phone exactly where it is.

“I’m on the back steps in Daddy’s Saints jacket,” she whispers, “and it isn’t even cold out here and I’m freezing, because I’m from here. Daddy hasn’t said a thing since the kick. Remy’s said everything. He blames the defense, the kicker, the Pope, and me, for wearing the wrong earrings. Josie’s got the television up so she doesn’t have to hear either one of them.” The step creaks. “For the record. It was strategy.”
“Overtime was strategy.”
“You don’t peak in December. You peak in February. Sean Payton is resting his *soul*.”
“He looked pretty awake at seventeen–nothing.”
“That’s when he started resting.” The step creaks. “I said a Memorare on the kick. Out loud. Our section heard me. Mr. Thibodeaux behind us took his hat off.”
“And?”
“And He said *wait*.” A breath down the line, all edges. “I hate *wait*. *No* I can argue with.”
He doesn’t say Providence. He’s been told.
“And don’t you argue with me in a whisper, it isn’t fair, I can’t get any volume on it.” A cup set down on wood. “Why is your grandmother asleep in the front room?”
“She won’t go up since Christmas. Ma tried. Pop offered to carry her.” He looks over at the chair. “She says the tree shouldn’t be by itself at night.”
On Dupre Street the step creaks, and for a little there’s only the house behind her, Remy and the television.
“Mémère says that about the dead,” Lena whispers. “You sit up with them.” And then, before it can turn into anything: “Tell her I said she’s right. What page?”
“Ninety-four.”
“Read me something.” And while he’s still turning back toward the tree for the light: “Not Percy. Me.”

So he tips the book to the tree and reads her her own handwriting, as low as he can go and still be heard. Her pencil is small and fast and runs uphill. A *no* on page thirty-one, under something Binx thinks about his secretary. “That stands.” A *ha* on fifty-eight. “That’s a good *ha*. I remember that *ha*.” *Oh, honey*, beside Binx on the Gentilly bus; that one gets nothing from her but the cup picked up off the step, and a drink, and the cup set down.
On page eighty-six, beside Kate, she wrote *spoiled* and underlined it twice.
“Oh, no.”
“Twice.”

“I was seventeen.” Two yards over on Dupre Street a dog barks and quits. “I was seventeen and I was *wrong* about Kate. I thought she was a rich girl having a mood in a nice house. She’s the only person in that house who says out loud she’s in trouble. Everybody else is polishing the silver.”
“Aunt Emily isn’t polishing anything. Aunt Emily’s holding the house up.”
“You *would* take Aunt Emily.”
“You did too.” He turns back to find it in the light, the big speech in the study near the end. “Right here. You wrote *Mémère*.”
What comes down the line would have been a shriek with any air behind it. “Lord have mercy. Don’t you *ever* tell her.”
“Were you wrong?”

“Half.” The step creaks as she settles in to do it properly. “Mémère’s got the silver *and* the rosary. Aunt Emily’s only got the silver. She’s magnificent and she’s wrong. She’s a pagan with good silver. She thinks the world’s going down and all that’s left is to go down like a lady.”
“She’s got a code. She keeps it when it costs her. You always know where the line is with her. Binx doesn’t have a line. Binx has the movies.”

“Binx has a *search*. Aunt Emily quit looking around 1918. A code is what you keep when you’ve stopped expecting anybody to come, Jack. That isn’t faith. That’s beautiful manners at the end of the world.”
“At the end of the world I’d take her over Binx.”
“So would I. In a fight. Not to Mass.”
“Percy gave her the best speech in the book.”
“Percy loves her the way you love the house you grew up in,” Lena says. “And then you move out.”
“Or you stay and fix the roof.”

She laughs the only way a whisper lets you, in short breaths against the phone, and it goes on long enough that he looks over at his grandmother to make sure. Nonna sleeps. The argument doesn’t get scored.
“What’s Binx doing now?” she says. “Where you are.”
“Thinking about his secretary.”
“That’s every page. Don’t you dare read the end first.”
“I never read the end first.”
“Then don’t start with this one. I’ll know. I’ll hear it in your voice.”
“Binx would hate it here,” he says. “Youngstown in December. It’s nothing but everydayness. Salt and the Browns.”
“Binx would *love* it there. Everybody in that town is on the search, Jack. Every man in that bar on Market Street where you watched us lose.” The step creaks. “They just call it the Browns.”

“Tomorrow’s the Innocents,” she whispers. “Mama goes to the seven o’clock every year. Every year since I can remember.” The screen door, very softly, behind her. “I never asked why.” And she goes on to something else before he can say anything: Josie’s science project, which is a volcano, and has been a volcano three years running, and has erupted at one time or another in every room of the house.
“And how was yours?” she says. “Besides the short form.”
Across the rug Nonna breathes in, and out, the long way.

response: “My dad went in today,” he whispers. “First time.”
“First time since —?”
“Ever.”
The screen door, very quietly, as she leans back against it. “Tell me.”

So he tells her. The radio quitting in the middle of a man’s sentence when his father turned the key. The Browns hat folded in half and put inside his coat. *Where do I stand?*, between the two steel doors, low, so the girls wouldn’t hear, and Ma not turning around. Danny standing up. *They play Oakland at four. — They’ll lose. — They won’t.* The coffee with cream and two sugars, the way Danny took it at fifteen, and Danny drinking it black now, and drinking this one anyway. *It’s good, Pop.* His father’s hand out across the bolted table at the end, and Danny looking at it, and taking it.
She doesn’t say anything clever. She doesn’t say anything at all until he’s finished, and not for a little after that either, with the house going on behind her.
“And Danny drank it.”
“Yeah.”
“Of course he did.”

response: “We went to see my brother,” he whispers. “All of us.”
“Rosie too?”

“Rosie said grace.” He does it for her the way Rosie did it, fast, a week of practice in the bathroom mirror behind it — *bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, and Danny, and Nonna’s hand* — and leaves off the end.
“What did y’all eat?”
“Honey buns. Out of a machine. Ma dealt out paper napkins from home like it was Thanksgiving.”

“Your mama is a saint and I will hear nothing else.” She asks the right small things after that — was it warm in there, did Gina behave, did Danny laugh — and he says yes, and no, and yes. He leaves his father out of it.

choices.text: “My brother laughed at my love life till a guard looked over.”
choices.key: Holy Family Sunday, whispering so you wouldn’t wake Nonna, you told Lena your brother laughed at your love life till a guard looked over.
response: “My brother laughed at my love life,” he whispers, “till a guard looked over.”
“Your *love* life.”
“What there is of it.”
The screen door; a breath on the steps. “I’d pay to see that guard.”
“He had a newspaper. He put it down.”

“Good for him. Somebody in that room had sense.” And she wants to know what they ate, and did Rosie go, and he tells her the honey buns and the paper napkins Ma brought from home, and leaves the rest where it is.

choices.key: Holy Family Sunday, whispering so you wouldn’t wake Nonna, you told Lena your Sunday was fine. Long.
response: “Fine,” he whispers. “Long.”
“Fine,” she whispers, the way you put something back on a shelf. He hears the cup come up off the step, and go down again.

“Well,” she says. “Ours was long too.” And she tells him about the Dome instead: Remy’s face paint coming off on the man in front of him in the fourth quarter, the man turning around to say something and seeing Remy’s face and deciding against it.

body: After that it’s the warm part, and none of it matters, and it goes on past midnight. She has the 8-Ball on the step beside her — she brought it out with the coffee — and she asks it whether the Saints are resting, and he hears the blue water go around in it and the wait while the answer floats up out of the dark.
“*Signs point to yes*,” she whispers.
“It always agrees with you.”
“It knows who has custody.”

She whispers him what Mémère has already decided about New Year’s, which came down at supper and is final. Black-eyed peas and cabbage on the first, peas for luck and cabbage for money, and everybody eats both, Lucille in spirit. No sweeping on New Year’s Day, or you sweep the luck out the front door. Every light in the house on at midnight, so the year can find the place. And Remy is not to be handed anything that lights.
“That last one’s Mama’s,” Lena says. “Mémère just nodded.”

And if Minnesota loses tomorrow night, she tells him, they get home field anyway, resting or not, so Daddy has announced he’ll be praying for the Chicago Bears. “He has never prayed for the Bears in his life. He doesn’t know how. He asked me what you say to God about Chicago.”
“What’d you tell him?”
“I told him the truth. Nobody knows.”
Across the rug Nonna turns over in her chair, as far as a chair allows, and says something into the wing of it, low and clear, in Calabrese.
“*Antò. Statti zitto.*”
Then she’s breathing again, slow, the long way out.
“What did she say?” Lena whispers.
“I don’t know.”
“Liar.”
He tells her about the program in the garage, the Browns and the Colts in 1964, hung up in a freezer bag with the thumbtacks through the corners of the bag so they won’t touch it.
“In a *freezer bag*,” Lena says. “Your daddy is a romantic.”
“Don’t tell him.”

“Who would I tell? Mémère?” Somewhere on Dupre Street a car goes by slow, and she waits for it to pass, as if it could hear. “Daddy sat in his seat after the kick till they turned the field lights down. He does that when they lose. He says you don’t walk out in the middle of a funeral.”
“Have you still got my tin?” she says.
“In the Carhartt.”
“Count them.”
“I counted them Christmas Eve.”

“Count them again. I’m not asking for me. I’m asking for the tin.” He gets up off the rug without a sound, more or less, and finds the Carhartt on the hook in the hall, and comes back with the tin, and opens it in the tree light on his knee and counts them with one finger so she can hear the filters tick against the lid.
“Eleven.”
“Eleven,” she says. “Don’t you smoke one up there without me. It doesn’t count in Ohio. It’s just smoking.”

By half past twelve his ear is hot from the phone and his legs have gone to sleep on the rug, and he doesn’t move either one. They do the rest of the hour on nothing. Josie gave Remy a purple Snuggie for Christmas as a joke, and he hasn’t taken it off since, and wore it to the game under his jersey. Whether three straight in December is a sign or a cruelty: a cruelty, she says; he says a sign. Whether the bathtub Madonna in the side yard minds the snow on her shoulders. (She doesn’t, Lena rules. She’s from Nazareth. She’s just never seen it.)
At two minutes to one by the RAZR she stops in the middle of nothing.
“I have to go,” she whispers. “Julian calls at ten his time.”

body.text: Before she goes: “Tell your daddy —” and she stops. “No. Don’t tell him anything. I’m just glad.”

body: “Goodnight, Jack.”
She hangs up first.

He sits on the rug in the light off the tree with the phone shut in his hand. Four feet away his grandmother breathes in, and out, a long way out. The furnace has quit under the floor, and the ornaments on the low branches have stopped turning.

s09a.slug: TUESDAY · 5:40 PM · THE SILVERADO, A SUPERMARKET LOT ON MARKET STREET
body: It’s been dark since five. The lot lights have come on orange over the slush, and the Silverado sits under one of them two rows back from the cart corral, engine running for the heater. Ma’s list is on the dash in her school-office capitals — MILK, ITALIAN BREAD, EGGS (LARGE) — and under it, in his father’s pencil, 2 TICKETS. Jack hasn’t gone in yet. Across the lot the doors keep opening on the bright inside of the store and letting people out with New Year’s in their carts, cases of pop, sleeves of plastic cups, a woman with three heads of cabbage in her arms like she’s carrying a baby.
At twenty to six the RAZR goes on the seat beside him. LENA.
“Home field,” she says, before he’s got it all the way to his ear.
“What?”
“*Home field.* Chicago beat the Vikings in overtime last night, so it comes through the Dome the whole way. Every game till Miami. Resting was *strategy*. Tell your daddy.”

He has never seen Broussard’s Seafood. He has it built anyway, out of four months of her talking: the long white cases of ice, the prices in grease pencil on the glass, her father’s Saints calendar over the register with the games crossed off in red. Behind her now it’s that, on Banks Street, the week after Christmas. The ice machine lets go of a load into its bin with a crash. A woman wants four dozen oysters for New Year’s and wants them big. Somewhere back of the register a radio is playing a record older than his father, a man singing the blues in a girl’s voice and then, for no reason anybody ever explained, a frog’s.

“I’m on the register,” she says. “I’m always on the register this week, every year since I could reach the drawer. Luc did it before me, and Remy did it for one afternoon in 2004, and we don’t talk about that afternoon. Four dozen, ma’am? Large? Yes, ma’am. Daddy, four dozen large.”

Then, to somebody on her end, at full Broussard volume: “Mr. Duplantier, I am not selling you shrimp at that price, I don’t care if you held me at my baptism. You dropped me at my baptism. Mama has pictures.” A man’s voice, aggrieved, and Tony’s from further back telling him to pay the girl. “Thank you, Mr. Duplantier. Happy New Year. Kiss Miss Rita.” And back into the phone, ordinary: “What is that noise?”
“My dad’s truck. I’m in a parking lot with my mother’s list.”
“Read it to me.”
He reads it to her off the dash. Milk. Italian bread. Eggs, large. Two tickets.
“*Italian* bread,” Lena says. “Y’all are lost up there. What tickets?”
“Lottery. My dad. Every Tuesday.”

“Tell him I said play the birthdays. Daddy plays all of ours and Mémère’s and Drew Brees’s, and he’s never won a dime, and he says that’s how you know it’s honest.” The register drawer rings open and shut. “He was in here at seven this morning lighting a candle in his head for a man named Jay Cutler. He wants to send him a sack of crawfish when they’re in season. He wants to know does Chicago have an address.” The ice machine. “Last night he watched it in the back office on the little TV with the foil on the antenna, and when Chicago scored in overtime he kissed the screen. On the mouth. Mémère saw. She hasn’t said a word to him since and it’s the happiest I’ve seen her all week.”
“The radio says Wednesday’s the coldest day of the year.”
“Colder than *now*? Jack. You’ll die. Wear the jacket. Wear two of the jacket.”
“We won Sunday,” Jack says. “Three straight.”
“Three.” She doesn’t sound one bit impressed, and she sounds pleased for him anyway. “Lord. Cleveland’s going to be impossible.”
Then a man’s voice comes up behind her, big enough to fill the market. “Is that the Ohio boy?”
“It’s the Ohio boy.”
“Tell him New Orleans is *resting*!”
“He heard you, Daddy. Algiers heard you.”

“And tell him —” closer now, right at her shoulder, cheerful, a man with nothing on his mind but a pot — “tell him I got a gumbo going for the musician Wednesday. *Real* one. Not that restaurant mess.”
“*Daddy.*”
“What? He’s a nice boy.”

Out in the lot a woman pushes a cart past the Silverado’s grille with a little boy riding in the basket, both of them in Steelers hats. The heater ticks. A plow goes by out on Market Street, and its orange light turns once across the dash and the list and is gone.
“Julian lands tomorrow at four,” Lena says. “Daddy’s taking him to the market first. To see the shrimp.”
The ice machine lets go of another load.
“I won’t call as much this week.”
“I know.”
On her end, a breath, and the register drawer, and the man on the record still going.
“…I’ll call.”

choices.text: “Tell your father the Browns are resting too.”
response: “Tell your father the Browns are resting too.”
She doesn’t have to. Tony has heard it from across the market. “*Lord*, son.” The oyster woman laughs, and Lena says she has a customer, and goes.
He sits in the lot with the list until the windshield fogs.
“Save me an oyster.”
“They don’t keep, Jack.”
“Then eat one for me.”
“I’ll eat *two*,” Lena says, and goes back to the four dozen.
He sits in the lot with the list until the windshield fogs.
“Go sell your shrimp, Broussard.”
“Yes, sir.” She’s gone on it, laughing at something the oyster woman said.
He sits in the lot with the list until the windshield fogs.

s10a.slug: THURSDAY · 7:38 AM · ST. BRIGID OF KILDARE, THE STEPS
body: Wednesday nothing came from New Orleans — not a text, all day, the first day since he got home.

Thursday the bells go for the end of the seven o’clock at St. Brigid’s and the doors let a dozen people out into a morning just starting to go gray over the South Side. Ma has gone to the seven o’clock on the last day of the year every year since she was a girl; this year he went with her. It was Saint Sylvester, a pope from the fourth century, and Father Dom read the beginning of John with his cough drop parked in his cheek — *the light shines in the darkness* — and in the prayers of the faithful, after the sick of the parish and before the dead, he prayed for the Americans killed in Afghanistan, and for their families, and the dozen of them answered him.

On the way out she stopped at the Mary altar, as she does on this morning, and lit a candle and put a dollar through the slot, and stood there with her gloves in one hand long enough that he went and stood with her. On the steps now Ma buttons her coat to the top and goes on down to the curb to warm up the truck. A salt truck comes up the street throwing its fan of grit at the parked cars. Over the roofs to the west the moon is still up, full and low and white, in a sky that’s already day around it.
At 7:38 the RAZR goes in his coat. LENA.
“I said I’d call,” she says.

She’s on the Moonwalk by the river, on a bench, with a café au lait and a bag of beignets from across the street, and the Quarter is empty: a man hosing down the flagstones in front of the café, a street sweeper going around Jackson Square, the pigeons. “This is the only hour it belongs to New Orleans,” she says. The barges for tonight are already anchored out in the river toward Algiers, and a tug is nosing at one of them. “Everybody on Dupre Street is asleep. Julian’s asleep in Remy’s room with his shoes lined up under the bed. Remy’s on the couch. He’s furious about it.”

“I left at six,” she says. “In Remy’s sneakers, they were by the door. I left a note on the icebox so Mama wouldn’t call Luc and have the Fifth District out looking for me.” The bag rustles. “Nobody’s down here this early but pigeons and people who work here and a few crazy people. And me. I’ve been coming since high school. It’s the only time the river sounds like a river.”
Jack sits down on the top step. The stone comes straight through his good pants.

“He peeled shrimp with Daddy for two hours yesterday and never once complained,” Lena says. “Daddy says he has the hands for it.” The bag rustles. “The gumbo happened. Mémère ironed the tablecloth twice.”
He doesn’t have anything for that. On her end the river goes on, and she waits a second for him, and then doesn’t.
The salt truck has turned at the corner and is coming back down the far side of the street.
“What is that?” she says.
“Salt truck. I’m on the church steps. Ma’s in the truck with the heater going.”
“Then go get in the truck, Jack.”
“In a minute.”

“Your mama’s going to think I’m a bad influence.” A paper bag, and something she tells somebody on her end — *merci, Mr. Ngo* — and back. “The waiter brought me a second order on the house because it’s the last day of the year. He’s been bringing me second orders since I was fourteen. He says I look like I need it. I have not ever needed it.” Powdered sugar, audibly. “I eat it anyway. It would be rude.”
“What are y’all doing tonight?” she says.

“Rosie’s midnight. At nine. Off a tape. Pots and pans on the porch.” He watches the truck’s grit hit the windshields of the cars along the curb. “Then a party. A guy from high school. His mother’s basement.”

“Look at you, going out.” A ship somewhere downriver sounds its horn, long. “Mémère has us on the levee by eleven-thirty in church clothes so the year can see we tried. Daddy’s bringing the chairs. Remy’s been told about the lighting things.”

Then, for half an hour, nothing that matters. Down by the river steps a man in a Saints toboggan is practicing the trumpet, scales, up and down and wrong at the same place every time, and she holds the phone out so Jack can hear him miss it. She’s got powdered sugar on her coat and on a pigeon that came too close, she says, and she isn’t brushing any of it off, because it’s Café du Monde sugar and that’s practically a sacramental. She wants to know what the Gospel was. He tells her John, the beginning, and she says the first line back to him from memory — “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” — and a gull goes over her, loud, and she says the next — “He was in the beginning with God” — and stops there, and drinks her coffee.

body.text: “Is your daddy going back?” “The third, maybe.” “Make him.”
“Did Rosie say grace again?” “Every meal. She’s added the Browns.”

body: Down at the curb the exhaust goes up white past his mother’s window.

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me. Holy Family Sunday she took Pop in. ‘You sit, Frank.’ Showed him the machines. Goes to the seven o’clock on the last day of every year; this year I went with her.

choices.key: The morning of New Year’s Eve, Lena called from the river at dawn, the way she said she would. You told her you were glad she did.
response: “I’m glad you called.”
“I said I would.” A gull; the river. “I don’t say things I don’t do, Jack.”
The beignets have gone cold, she says, and Mémère will want her at the market by eight, so she has to go.
“Happy New Year, Jack. Early. In case.”
She hangs up first. He stays on the step with the phone in his hand while the salt truck turns at the bottom of the street, and down at the curb his mother gives the horn a tap.

response: He lets her talk. The river at her end, a ship’s horn somewhere downstream, and her voice giving him the Quarter waking up one shutter at a time: the man with the hose finished, a praline shop rolling up its grate, the street sweeper on its second lap of the square. He says almost nothing. She doesn’t need him to.

She hangs up first. He stays on the step with the phone in his hand while the salt truck turns at the bottom of the street, and down at the curb his mother gives the horn a tap.

body.text: On the front steps in his coat, after the house has gone up. The tree is still on in the window behind him. The street is quiet except for a party two streets over that keeps letting the new year out its front door a few people at a time, and every time it does he hears it, somebody laughing, a car door, a name called down a driveway. His breath goes up past the porch light. Glenwood Avenue is salted end to end and there isn’t a car moving on it. Inside, the year has turned over, and everybody who was up for it has gone to bed.
body.else: On the sidewalk a block from home, walking. The South Side is still letting the new year off in pieces: a bottle rocket somewhere toward Market, a car going by with the windows down and the radio up, a man alone on his porch hitting a pot lid with a spoon because nobody told him to stop. The one beer is long gone. The salt crunches under his shoes, and up ahead on Glenwood the porch light is still on at his parents’ house, the only one on the block, left on for him. Every house on Glenwood is a house he could name the people in.

body: At a minute to one he has the phone out already, open in his glove, because he knows what time it is on the river. Her text from his midnight is still in the inbox, an hour old. The inside screen is the brightest thing on the street, the time across the top of it, and the time says 12:59.
It goes to 1:00, and the phone goes in his hand in the same second.

Not a minute after. Not at the end of the first rocket. On the levee they’d barely have the barges lit. Her whole family is out there in church clothes — Mémère, and her father with the chairs, and Remy not being handed anything that lights — and Julian beside her, who has never seen it. She must have had it typed before the year came, with her thumb on the key, and she sent it before she turned to any of them.

He knows what that means. It’s the first thing anybody learns about midnight: who you turn to. An hour ago, at his, he had both of them on the little screen, and he answered Skye first, and he did it on purpose. He chose. The clock on the RAZR says she did too.

body.text: They set the whole sky on fire over Algiers. Julian has never seen a city burn things on purpose. Daddy says it’s the only way to start a year. —L.

body: He takes the glove off his right hand with his teeth. The true answer to the first one is in him, all of it, and it doesn’t go on a keypad. Not to a levee, with Julian standing next to her. Not from this phone.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks, before anybody. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it.
